description:
This session moves from the Holy Spirit’s ministry into the course’s study of prayer. Wesam Saad first answers the question left open at the previous meeting: whether Christians may pray to the Holy Spirit. He distinguishes permission from the usual biblical pattern, encouraging prayer to the Father through Jesus Christ in the Spirit’s power while affirming the Spirit’s deity.

Saad then gathers the congregation’s practical questions about prayer. These include its difficulty, frequency, corporate and private expression, written prayers and the danger of legalism. Some receive preliminary discussion, while others are reserved for later sessions. His aim is for theological understanding to produce prayerful people and a prayerful church. In considering written prayers, he points to the Psalms and the care involved in preparing meaningful words for someone we love.

The main teaching concerns prayer’s purpose: reverent communion with God, expressing dependence, submission and trust rather than supplying information. Psalms 42, 84 and 63 portray thirst for God, joy in his presence and earnest desire to see his glory. Saad urges listeners to seek God himself above the benefits they hope to receive, letting that desire shape their approach to prayer.

questions.question: Does Saad regard prayer addressed to the Holy Spirit as sinful?
questions.answer: He affirms that the Holy Spirit is God and therefore does not treat addressing him in prayer as sinful. He nevertheless distinguishes what is permissible from the pattern he encourages Christians ordinarily to follow.

questions.question: What pattern of prayer does he encourage, and why?
questions.answer: He encourages prayer to the Father through Jesus Christ in the power of the Holy Spirit. He appeals to Jesus’ example and explains the Spirit’s work in helping believers, interceding for them and directing their attention to Christ.

questions.question: What does Saad want the extended discussion of prayer to accomplish?
questions.answer: He wants theological knowledge to change hearts and produce prayerful men and women. He invites practical questions so the course can address real obstacles, including difficulty praying, motives, legalism and the place of corporate prayer, while recognising that many answers will come in later sessions.

questions.question: How does he respond to the concern that writing a prayer is cheating?
questions.answer: He challenges that assumption by pointing to the written Psalms and comparing preparation with carefully composing words for a loved one. Thoughtful preparation can express care rather than dishonesty. He also recognises the value of freely speaking to God and leaves fuller discussion for later.

questions.question: Why is prayer more than giving God information?
questions.answer: God already knows everything. Saad presents prayer as reverent communion in which believers express submission to God’s sovereignty, trust his faithfulness, worship him and acknowledge their dependence on him as the giver of all things.

questions.question: What kind of desire does Psalm 42 teach listeners to bring to prayer?
questions.answer: Saad highlights the psalmist’s urgent thirst for the living God. The longing is deeper than a casual wish to feel better: the psalmist yearns to appear before God. Saad uses this to challenge a detached or merely habitual approach to communion with him.

questions.question: What does Psalm 84 add to the picture of longing for God?
questions.answer: The psalm describes delight in God’s dwelling places and the whole person singing for joy to the living God. Saad connects longing for God with the joy of being in his presence, rather than treating prayer only as a demanding duty.

questions.question: How does Psalm 63 help distinguish seeking God from seeking only his benefits?
questions.answer: Saad emphasises the psalmist’s personal attachment to God, earnest seeking and desire to see his power and glory. He does not dismiss the benefits of prayer, but places God himself above them as the supreme reason for entering his presence.
